newsitem.title: USA: Stocks coast to slightly lower close.
newsitem.headline: Stocks coast to slightly lower close.

text.p: Stock prices ended slightly lower Thursday as Wall Street turned cautious ahead of Friday's important jobs report for February.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 1.15 points at 6,944.70. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,253 to 1,205 on active volume of 522 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"It's amazing the Dow wasn't down more," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney. "You just didn't have any buyers today because you've got the moment of truth of the week tomorrow."

The cautious mood contrasted with Wednesday's session, when soothing comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan eased investors' fears that the central bank was planning some action to slow the stock market's rise and set off a rally of 93 points in the blue-chip Dow index.

But there was no exuberance in the market Thursday as investors braced for the possibility that a strong set of economic figures on Friday could prompt the Fed to pull the trigger on an interest rate increase.
"The stock market is struggling to get a true sense of the strength of the economy and what will be the course of Fed policy," said Charles White, managing director at Avatar Associates.
The bond market was also on guard prior to the jobs data. The key 30-year Treasury bond lost 22/32, sending its yield up to 6.88 percent from Wednesday's close of 6.83 percent.

According to economists surveyed by Reuters, the report is expected to show 230,000 new jobs were created in February, down from 271,000 in January, and the nation's unemployment rate is expected to edge down to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent.
Analysts said the market will look closely at the average hourly wage component of the report, which is seen rising by 0.4 percent from 0.1 percent a month ago.
"Nobody's doubting that the labour market is tight," White said. "Our focus will be on the wage number."
Despite a mostly tentative market, some stocks did stand out.
Oil companies were among the strongest performers. Texaco Inc. rose 2-1/8 to 103-7/8 and Chevron Corp. was up 1-1/8 to 66-1/2.
Technology stocks were weaker, with Oracle Corp. skidding 3-3/16 to 36-9/16 after UBS Securities cut its rating on the shares, citing uncertainty about Oracle's fiscal third quarter results.
The technology sell-off extended well beyond individual issues, however, dragging down a host of top-tier names.
Intel Corp. fell 4-1/8 to 145-3/8, Microsoft Corp. sank 3-1/8 to 97-3/4, Cisco Systems Inc. shed 2-1/4 to 54-5/8 and Dell Computer Corp. was off 1-1/4 to 73-7/8.
Great Western Financial Corp. rose 1-3/4 to 46-3/4 after agreeing to be acquired by Washington Mutual Savings Bank in a friendly $6.6 billion deal.

Washington Mutual's offer tops a $6.1 billion hostile bid by A.H. Ahmanson & Co. Ahmanson, the nation's largest savings and loan, said it remained committed to the deal, and analysts expect the firm will raise its bid. Ahmanson fell 1-1/4 to 40-3/4. Washington Mutual shares fell 1/4 to 53.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 13.66 points to 1,315.43.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks lost 3.43 to 798.56. The American Stock Exchange index slipped 0.57 to 660.31.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.43 to 420.24. The average share was down 5 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,639.678 down 19.215 or 0.25 percent.
